title: Common exception words: what they are and how to learn them
meta_description: Common exception words are words with letter and sound matches not yet taught as widely applicable. Find the odd part, then practise the word from memory.
hero_image_alt: A closed navy notebook, a navy pencil, a stack of blank white cards with a pink one on top, and a mug of tea on a pale wooden table.
content_html:
Common exception words are words whose spelling contains letter and sound matches that children have not yet been taught as widely applicable. The national curriculum for England uses the term for words that break the patterns pupils have learnt so far. Children usually learn them by noticing the unusual part of each word, then practising the whole word from memory.

Key takeaways

  • The national curriculum describes common exception words as words containing letter and sound matches that have not yet been taught as widely applicable, so the label depends on what a child has already learnt.
  • The curriculum says some words are exceptions in some accents but not in others, so a word that looks odd to one family may not sound odd to another.
  • The curriculum asks teachers to draw attention to the sound and letter matches in a word that do and do not fit what has been taught, which is a useful habit at home too.
  • One 2022 experiment with beginning readers found that children who actively processed a word's spelling learnt irregular words better than children who only looked at the word and said it.

What does “common exception word” mean?

A common exception word is a word that does not follow the spelling patterns children have been taught so far. The national curriculum defines the group by the letter and sound matches inside the words: they have not yet been taught as widely applicable, so a child cannot yet rely on a pattern to spell them.

The two halves of the name both do work, though the curriculum does not gloss them. Common suggests words children meet often in reading and writing, which would explain why they are named and listed in the spelling appendix. Exception marks the word as an exception to the rules a child has met, not as a word that no rule could ever explain.

If you want the wider background on why English spelling behaves like this, we have covered it in why English spelling is so hard for children to learn.

Why is a word an exception for one child and not another?

A word is an exception only in relation to what has been taught, which is why the same word can feel easy for one child and puzzling for another. The curriculum's definition rests on matches that have not yet been taught. A child who has met a particular spelling of a sound in several words may find a word containing it unremarkable. A child who has not will find it arbitrary.

Accent adds another layer. The Year 2 notes in the spelling appendix say: “Some words are exceptions in some accents but not in others.” The appendix gives past, last, fast, path and bath as words that are not exceptions in accents where the a is pronounced as it is in cat.

So a child's difficulty with a word does not by itself show that they have missed something. The word may simply sit awkwardly against how they say it.

Do common exception words have a rule?

Some words do not have a rule that helps, and the curriculum says so plainly. In its introduction, the spelling appendix explains that choosing the right letter or letters depends on pupils having made a conscious effort to learn the words, or having absorbed them less consciously through reading. In its suffix guidance for Years 5 and 6 it says that there are many words where the guidance does not help and those words just have to be learnt.

That does not mean every unusual word is a complete mystery. Often most of a word behaves normally and only one part does not. The curriculum's wording for Year 1 shows the idea: pupils' attention should be drawn to the sound and letter matches that do and do not fit in with what has been taught so far. In plain terms, the child is helped to see which part of the word is ordinary and which part is the exception.

How do children learn common exception words?

Children learn common exception words by giving the spelling active attention, not just by hearing the word said. The best evidence we found for this is narrow, so it is worth setting out what it did and did not measure.

In 2022 Colenbrander and colleagues, writing in Scientific Studies of Reading, compared three ways of teaching irregular words to eighty five Kindergarten children who were beginning to read. Each child was taught twelve irregular words over three sessions, with teaching time and the number of times they met each word held equal. Two of the methods, called Look and Spell and mispronunciation correction, produced better learning of the taught words than the third, called Look and Say, and than a wait list control. The authors conclude that active processing of a word's spelling is crucial for learning irregular words.

Four limits apply. The children were beginning readers. The outcomes were reading the words aloud and choosing the correct spelling from options, not writing words from memory. There was no evidence that learning carried over to words that had not been taught. And the two better methods did not differ from each other, with the authors saying further research is needed to see whether they come apart over longer training. The study supports the narrow claim that attention to the spelling of an irregular word helps. It does not tell us how many times a word needs practising, or which method suits a seven year old.

What can a parent do at home?

A parent can turn the curriculum's own advice into a short routine. None of what follows comes from a study of families; it is reasoning from the sources above rather than a finding from any of them.

  • Find the unusual part before practising. Look at the word with your child and ask which part behaves normally and which part does not. The curriculum's wording for Year 1 describes teachers doing exactly this, and the habit takes seconds.
  • Keep the unusual part in view while the child practises. The Colenbrander experiment points to attention to the spelling mattering more than repetition by ear, so a child who looks closely at the tricky part is doing something useful.
  • Then ask the child to write the whole word from memory. Looking, covering, writing and checking asks a child to recall the spelling and not simply copy it. Our page on look, cover, write, check sets out the four steps.
  • Come back to the word on another day. A word that a child can spell once, straight after seeing it, has not necessarily stuck. Our explanation of how spelling sticks covers why practice spread over different days is worth the extra effort.

What if a child keeps getting the same word wrong?

A child who keeps misspelling the same exception word is usually getting one part of it wrong, and finding that part is more useful than more repetition of the whole word. Look at the wrong spellings for a pattern. If every attempt differs in the same place, that is the part to point at.

The curriculum also asks teachers to keep drawing attention to the relationships between sounds and letters, even where those relationships are unusual. That is a reminder that an odd spelling is still a spelling of the sounds in the word, not an arbitrary string of letters.

If the same word keeps going wrong for weeks, your child's teacher can tell you whether it is one the class is working on and what approach the school uses.

FAQ

What are common exception words?

Common exception words are words that contain letter and sound matches which have not yet been taught as widely applicable. The national curriculum for England names them in its spelling appendix.

Are the same words exceptions in every school?

The curriculum's own notes say that some words are exceptions in some accents but not in others. Which words a child practises each week is set by the school, so your child's teacher can tell you what the class is learning.

Does my child have to learn them by heart?

For some words, yes. The national curriculum says that choosing the right letters often depends on a conscious effort to learn the words, and, in its suffix guidance for Years 5 and 6, that there are many words where the guidance does not help. It does not say the learning has to be dull or repeated many times.

How many exception words should we practise at once?

We did not find a source that sets a number. The practical limit is usually the child's patience and the length of the school's list, so a short, regular session is a reasonable starting point.

If you would like a short daily way to practise the words your child brings home, you can find Spelling Nest here, built by a teacher and parent.
